subject: COM
label: Grade 01
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 01 Computing, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Parts of a computer
modules.outcome: name the screen, keyboard, mouse and their jobs
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Parts of a computer', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: name the screen, keyboard, mouse and their jobs. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: See it: watch or try the skill in 'Parts of a computer' on a teacher screen or a safe device.
Name the parts: write the key words and what each part does.
Use it: name the screen, keyboard, mouse and their jobs. Save your work in a named file or folder.
Test and fix: run it, find one fault, correct it, and note what you changed.
modules.example: Solved: Input: keyboard, mouse. Output: screen, printer. Processing: CPU. Storage: hard drive. Press a key (input), the screen shows a letter (output). Method: Model run for 'Parts of a computer'. Goal in one sentence. Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Name the screen, keyboard, mouse and their jobs: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Look at the screen. The screen is the part that shows pictures, words and games. It works like a window into the computer. Point to it. Keep your fingers off the glass, because fingerprints make it hard to see, and keep drinks far away from it.

Step 2, Meet the keyboard. The keyboard has keys for letters, numbers and a long space bar. There are 26 letter keys, one for each letter of the alphabet. We use the keyboard to type. Find the keys c, a and t and press them one at a time, gently, to make the word cat.

Step 3, Hold the mouse. The mouse sits on the table and slides to move the little arrow, called the pointer, on the screen. A mouse has two buttons. Press the left button once, called a click, to choose something. Slide slowly, and stop on a picture before you click.

Step 4, Match each part to its job. Screen: we see. Keyboard: we type letters and numbers. Mouse: we point and click. Say the pairs aloud: the screen shows, the keyboard types, the mouse clicks. Point to each part on a real computer or a picture as you say it.

Step 5, Use the parts together. Sit with feet on the floor and clean hands. Look at the screen, slide the mouse so the pointer lands on a star picture, click once, then use the keyboard to type your first name. Each part did its own job, one after another.

Step 6, Your turn: which part do you use to type your name, which to see a picture, and which to click a button? Answer: the keyboard to type your name, the screen to see a picture, and the mouse to click a button.

modules.standard: Click, drag and type letters and my name: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Sit and set up: Amina sits with both feet on the floor, the screen at eye level, and one hand on the mouse. She finds the pointer arrow on the screen and moves the mouse slowly until the arrow touches the big green square.

Step 2, Click: With the arrow on the green square, Amina presses the left button once and lets go. The square turns yellow. One quick press is a click. She says 'click' aloud each time to remember the single press.

Step 3, Drag: Amina puts the arrow on a red ball, holds the left button down, slides the mouse to the basket on the right, then lets go. The ball drops into the basket. Hold, move, release is called dragging.

Step 4, Find letters: Her teacher shows a box and the letters A, M, I, N. Amina looks at the keyboard, finds the A key on the left side of the middle row, and presses it once. An 'a' appears in the box.
Step 5, Type the name: She holds the Shift key with her little finger while pressing A to make a capital, so the first letter is right. Next come m, i, n, a. The screen shows Amina, five letters.

Step 6, Check and fix: She reads the screen letter by letter, touching each one with the pointer: A-m-i-n-a. All five match. If a letter were wrong she would press Backspace once to remove the last letter and type again.

Your turn: Your name is Omar. Click the blue button, drag a star into a box, then type your name with a capital O. Model answer: O comes from Shift plus the O key, then m, a, r. The screen shows Omar, four letters, and the star sits inside the box.

Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Make a simple picture with a drawing tool: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Open the tool: Lina clicks the drawing tool icon, a paintbrush on the desktop. A white page opens with a row of colour squares at the top and a pencil, a brush and an eraser on the left side.

Step 2, Pick a colour and tool: She clicks the yellow square, then the brush. The pointer changes to a small dot. Yellow is now the colour she will draw with, so everything she paints from here will be yellow.

Step 3, Draw the sun: Holding the left button down, Lina moves the mouse in a slow circle in the top corner. When the circle joins up she lets go. A yellow round sun appears. She adds five short lines around it for rays.

Step 4, Change colour for the house: She clicks the red square and draws a square box in the middle of the page for the house wall. Then she clicks brown and draws a triangle on top for the roof, making a simple house.

Step 5, Fix a mistake: One ray crossed the roof. Lina clicks the eraser tool, rubs over only that crossing line, and the white page shows again. She switches back to the yellow brush and draws the ray shorter.

Step 6, Save: Lina clicks the save button, types the name 'my house' and presses Enter. The tool shows 'my house' at the top. She now has a picture with a sun, a house and a roof that she can open tomorrow.

Your turn: Draw a tree with a brown trunk and a green top, then erase one mistake and save it as 'tree'. Model answer: pick brown and draw a thin tall rectangle, pick green and draw a round top, use the eraser on any stray mark, then save with the name tree.

modules.title: Staying safe with screens
modules.outcome: follow simple rules for screen time and sharing
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Staying safe with screens', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: follow simple rules for screen time and sharing. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: See it: watch or try the skill in 'Staying safe with screens' on a teacher screen or a safe device.
Name the parts: write the key words and what each part does.
Use it: follow simple rules for screen time and sharing. Save your work in a named file or folder.
Test and fix: run it, find one fault, correct it, and note what you changed.
modules.example: Solved: Never share your password, address or school name. If a stranger messages you: do not reply, close it, tell a trusted adult. Strong password: three random words plus a number. Method: Model run for 'Staying safe with screens'. Goal in one sentence. Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Follow simple rules for screen time and sharing: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Ask first. Screens are fun, but eyes and bodies need a rest. Before you use a tablet or computer, ask a grown-up. Your family decides how long, for example one hour after school. A kitchen timer helps you stop when it rings, with no arguing.

Step 2, Take screen breaks. After a short time, look away from the screen at something far away, like a tree outside, for 20 seconds. Sit with your back straight and the screen about an arm's length away. Stand up, stretch your arms up high and drink some water.

Step 3, Know what stays private. Never type or say your full name, home address, phone number, school name or passwords to anyone online. Photos of your house or school uniform tell people where you are. Before you share anything, show a grown-up first and ask if it is safe.

Step 4, Use the Stop, Ask, Tell rule. If a picture is scary or a message is unkind, stop looking and close the screen or turn it off. Ask a grown-up what to do. Tell a trusted grown-up, such as a parent or teacher, straight away. You will never be in trouble for telling.

Step 5, Balance the day. Plan 1 hour of screen time, then play outside, read a book, help at home and sleep. In one week one hour a day is 7 hours of screen time. Draw a picture of your day with the screen as only one small part of it.
Step 6, Your turn: a game asks, What is your home address? What do you do? Answer: do not type it, stop and ask a grown-up, because your address is private. Tell the grown-up about the question.
